in_text_mentions: According to the St. James University Hospital MRI classification, the largest proportion of patients were categorized as grade 4 (55.8%) (Figure 5), followed by grade 3 (15.4%) (Figure 6), grade 2 (13.5%), grade 0 (9.6%), grade 1 (3.8%) (Figure 7), and grade 5 (1.9%) (Table 3). Surgical grading was consistent with imaging findings, with grade 4 being the most common (53.8%) (Table 4). MRI findings demonstrated excellent correlation with intraoperative findings in 88.5% of cases, with a statistically significant level of agreement (Cohen’s kappa = 0.820, p < 0.001).

in_text_mentions: eater engagement in care have been associated with improved outcomes in chronic conditions such as Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). In perianal Crohn’s disease (pCD), a severe phenotype of Crohn’s disease (CD), complex fistulae can cause substantial social and occupational burden [8]. Management often requires lifelong repeated imaging, with MRI recommended by both European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation (ECCO) and the European Society for Gastrointestinal and Abdominal Radiology (ESGAR) as the gold standard modality [9,10]. An example MRI of a complex perianal fistula is shown in Figure 1.

panels.figure_caption: Short tau inversion recovery sequence showing perianal fistula Coronal (A and B) and Axial (C and D) short tau inversion recovery images of a 37-year-old male demonstrating a linear intersphincteric perianal fistula (white arrow) with its internal opening at 5'o clock position
in_text_mentions: tivity is almost comparable to the one reported by another study [17]. STIR sequences are commonly used for the anatomical regions that have a high fat content where the important aspect of inversion recovery can be applied [18]. The visualization of a fistulous tract depends upon their content as well as the degree of inflammation. STIR suppresses the signals of adjacent fat and provides a good contrast to identify the fistula easily. In the active disease phase, the fistula usually contains granulation tissue with fluid and is usually seen as a linear tract of high signal on STIR (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (a, b, c, d, e). a: Conventional fistulogram shows branching left perianal fistula communicating with rectum in Crohn's disease case; real patient radiology showing target disease manifestation, vocab has no fistulogram tract term so captured in proposed_findings. b: Coronal T1W MRI shows bilateral ischiorectal fistula tracts in Crohn's perianal fistula case, matching fistula tract on MRI vocabulary. c: Coronal FS T2W MRI shows transsphincteric and extrasphincteric tracts in same Crohn's fistula patient, direct MRI tract manifestation. d: Axial FS T2W MRI shows bilateral ischiorectal abscesses communicating across midline with internal opening; abscess component has no MRI abscess term in vocab so in proposed, communicating tract supports MRI tract finding. e: Axial postcontrast T1W MRI depicts enhancement of the horseshoe abscess in same Crohn's perianal fistula/abscess case; no MRI abscess finding_key in vocab so captured as proposed_findings, still...

panels.figure_caption: Crohn's disease with extrasphincteric fistulae. Conventional fistulogram (a) shows a branching left perianal fistula (long arrow), communicating with the rectum (short arrow). Coronal T1W image (b) depicts bilateral ischiorectal tracts (arrows). Coronal fat-saturated T2W image (c) depicts one transsphincteric tract interrupting the right external sphincter (arrow), the two other tracts being extrasphincteric. Axial fat-saturated T2W image (d) shows bilateral ischiorectal abscesses communicating across the midline with a posterior internal opening at 6 o'clock position (arrow). Axial postcontrast T1W image (e) depicts enhancement of the horseshoe abscess (arrow)
in_text_mentions: Three patients had a primary or recurrent perianal fistula with associated Crohn's disease [Figure 2]. Two of these three cases had multiple fistulae and all three had abscess formation [Figure 2d and e]. Of the remaining 32 patients without Crohn's disease, 24 had a primary fistula and, of these, seven had previously undergone perianal abscess drainage. Eight patients had undergone previous fistula surgery and had presented with a recurrence.

A: Preoperative MRI panel showing abnormal signal at internal opening of low intersphincteric complex anal fistula, consistent with target disease. B: Preoperative MRI panel showing two intersphincteric fistula tracts, consistent with low-position intersphincteric complex anal fistula.
panels.attribution_text: Chen et al. Postoperative bleeding complicated by hemophilia A following anal fistula surgery: A case report.. Medicine 2025. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000044962. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative MRI of the anal canal with plain scan, diffusion, and dynamic enhancement images: (A) an abnormal signal is observed at the 5 o’clock position (lithotomy position) within the internal anal sphincter, suggestive of the fistula’s internal opening. (B) Approximately 3.6 cm from the anal verge, 2 fistula tracks are seen descending through the intersphincteric branch at the 5 o’clock and 7 o’clock positions. Lithotomy position: the anal canal is conceptualized as the center of a clock face, with the 12 o’clock position corresponding to the patient’s ventral side (anterior) and the 6 o’clock position corresponding to the patient’s dorsal side (posterior). MRI = magnetic resonance imaging.
in_text_mentions: 19.10 %. No significant abnormalities were observed in the infection disease quantitative tests or blood biochemistry. MRI of the anal canal, including plain scan, diffusion, and dynamic enhancement, showed abnormal signals at the 5 o’clock position in the anal sphincter (internal opening), approximately 3.6 cm from the anal margin. Two fistula tracts (at 5 o’clock and 7 o’clock) were visualized, extending downward through the intersphincteric branches, with the external opening at the gluteal skin. The findings are consistent with a low-position intersphincteric complex anal fistula (Fig. 1).

in_text_mentions: ed above can be complicated by secondary tracks. Supralevator, ischioanal and horseshoe extensions are common. Horseshoe extensions are circular extensions to both sides of the internal opening (Fig. 7). Any type of fistula may show a circumferential spread, but a typical horseshoe-shaped fistula has two tracts and one internal opening, often in the midline posteriorly at the level of the inferior border of the puborectalis muscle. in_text_mentions: The next common type, or trans-sphincteric type, occurs when the track courses through the external sphincter muscle, usually involving the ischioanal fossa (Fig. 4). This should not necessarily mean that that the fistula has traversed the external sphincter. The level at which the external sphincter complex is traversed is most often at the mid-anal canal level and the internal opening is usually at around 6 o’clock, at the level of dentate line. B: Axial DWI in same patient showing fistula tract in left ischioanal fossa; internal orifice almost invisible but tract visible, still shows MRI manifestation of anorectal fistula. panels.figure_caption: MR images of a 49-year-old man with a transsphincteric perianal fistula. (A) The internal orifice (thin arrow) is identified in the 3 o’clock direction, and the fistula tract (thick arrow) is noted in the left ischioanal fossa on axial fat suppressed T2-weighted imaging (FS T2WI). (B) The internal orifice (thin arrow) is almost invisible on axial diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and the fistula tract (thick arrow) is noted in the left ischioanal fossa. (C) The internal orifice (thin arrow) is identified in the 3 o’clock direction, and the fistula tract (thick arrow) is noted in the left ischioanal fossa on axial fat suppressed T1-weighted imaging with contrast enhanced (FS T1WI+CE). It shows not only the enhancement of the fistula tract, but also the enhancement of the inflammatory infection tissue (curved arrow) around the fistula. It is recorded a slightly higher confidence score for lesion conspicuity on FS T2WI than on FS T1WI+CE.
in_text_mentions: The conspicuity of the fistula was higher for the set of FS T2WI+DWI and FS T1WI+CE than that of FS T2WI or DWI. However, there was no significant differences between the sets of FS T2WI+DWI and FS T1WI+CE (Table 3, Figs. 1 and 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial FS T2WI in 23-year-old man with horseshoe fistula showing internal orifice and fistula tract around anal canal, matching fistula tract on MRI. B: Axial DWI in same patient showing internal orifice and horseshoe fistula tract, specific MRI manifestation of fistula-in-ano. C: Contrast-enhanced FS T1WI shows visible fistula tract in horseshoe fistula case, despite internal orifice not identified. D: ADC map in same horseshoe fistula patient showing internal orifice and fistula tract, specific MRI manifestation.
panels.attribution_text: Gu et al. A comparable method to Gd-contrast enhancement in the preoperative evaluation of anal fistula.. Medicine 2019. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000017807. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: MR images of a 23-year-old man with a horseshoe fistula. (A) The internal orifice (thin arrow) is identified in the 5 o’clock direction, and the fistula tract (thick arrow) is noted around the anal canal on axial fat suppressed T2-weighted imaging (FS T2WI). (B, D) The internal orifice (thin arrow) and fistula tract (thick arrow) are both obviously showed on axial diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and the corresponding map of apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). (C) The internal orifice is not identified on axial fat suppressed T1-weighted imaging with contrast enhanced (FS T1WI+CE), which maybe the result of the enhancement of the internal orifice and the mocosa at the same time. The fistula tract is visible (thick arrow).
in_text_mentions: ucosa of the internal sphincter are not uniform in normal people actually. Sometimes local thickening of the mucosa shows high signal on FS T2WI sequence. Small vessels around the anas can also show high signal like dot or strip, which are similar to the signal of internal orifice. It is often difficult to distinguish. Although contrast enhancement (CE) can improve the detection rate of the internal orifice, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish from the perianal blood vessels or mucosa. However, the combination of DWI sequence becomes essential to increase the diagnostic accuracy (Fig. 3).

panels.attribution_text: Khanduri et al. Seeing Beyond the Tract: The Superiority of 3 Tesla (3T) MRI Over X-ray Fistulography in Perianal Fistula Evaluation.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.93825. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: MRI fistulogram demonstrating a St. James grade 3 perianal fistula MRI: magnetic resonance imaging; STIR: short tau inversion recovery Axial (A), sagittal (B), T2-weighted, coronal STIR (C), and axial (D) T1-weighted images reveal a transsphincteric fistulous tract (orange arrows) extending through both the internal and external sphincters into the ischioanal fossa. Mild surrounding inflammation is noted without associated abscess or secondary extensions (C)
in_text_mentions: According to the St. James University Hospital MRI classification, the largest proportion of patients were categorized as grade 4 (55.8%) (Figure 5), followed by grade 3 (15.4%) (Figure 6), grade 2 (13.5%), grade 0 (9.6%), grade 1 (3.8%) (Figure 7), and grade 5 (1.9%) (Table 3). Surgical grading was consistent with imaging findings, with grade 4 being the most common (53.8%) (Table 4). MRI findings demonstrated excellent correlation with intraoperative findings in 88.5% of cases, with a statistically significant level of agreement (Cohen’s kappa = 0.820, p < 0.001).

panels.attribution_text: Yang et al. Preoperative assessment of fistula-in-ano using SonoVue enhancement during three-dimensional transperineal ultrasound.. Gastroenterology report 2024. doi:10.1093/gastro/goae002. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Suprasphincteric fistula and internal opening. (A) Position relationship between anal fistula and sphincter. (B) Fistula imaging under SVE 3D-TPUS. (C) Internal opening and fistula imaging under SVE 3D-TPUS. SVE 3D-TPUS, SonoVue 3D transperineal ultrasound.
in_text_mentions: Among the 60 patients who underwent surgery, 68 internal openings were found during surgery (Figure 5). The number of preoperatively detected internal openings was significantly higher by SVE 3D-TPUS than by 3D-TPUS [97.1% (66/68) vs 80.9% (55/68), P = 0.001, Table 1]. Compared with 3D-TPUS, SVE 3D-TPUS had a higher accuracy in detecting internal openings in the fistulae.

study, SVE 3D-TPUS was tolerated well by all 60 patients and had a significantly higher accuracy in detecting the location of the internal opening compared with that of 3D-TPUS. Moreover, the tomographic ultrasound imaging technique was found to be helpful in tracing the pathway of the fistulae and internal openings (Figures 4 and 5) and improved the diagnostic accuracy. In this study, the accuracy of complexity classification was significantly higher with SVE 3D-TPUS than with 3D-TPUS. Therefore, routine use of SVE during 3D-TPUS may be recommended for the detection of complex anal fistulae.

in_text_mentions: According to the St. James University Hospital MRI classification, the largest proportion of patients were categorized as grade 4 (55.8%) (Figure 5), followed by grade 3 (15.4%) (Figure 6), grade 2 (13.5%), grade 0 (9.6%), grade 1 (3.8%) (Figure 7), and grade 5 (1.9%) (Table 3). Surgical grading was consistent with imaging findings, with grade 4 being the most common (53.8%) (Table 4). MRI findings demonstrated excellent correlation with intraoperative findings in 88.5% of cases, with a statistically significant level of agreement (Cohen’s kappa = 0.820, p < 0.001).

findings.label: Fistulous tract on MRI fistula protocol

panels.rationale: Single axial MRI with arrows showing complex fistulous tract and bilateral ischiorectal abscesses in a patient with cryptoglandular perianal abscess and horseshoe fistula; matches target disease anorectal_abscess_fistula.
panels.attribution_text: Lyons et al. Refractory Cryptoglandular Perianal Abscess and Fistulas Due to Mycobacterium avium Infection in an Immunocompetent Adult.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.67827. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: MRI demonstrating complex fistula (yellow) with bilateral (L > R), evolving ischiorectal abscesses (white). During the patient’s first procedure at our institution, surgeons located the internal opening of the abscess in the posterior midline, just distal to the dentate line. It was found to have extension from the posterior midline to both the left and right.
in_text_mentions: cellulitis progressed, and she developed an abscess. An incision and drainage (I&D) was performed, but unfortunately, no intraoperative cultures were sent. Over a span of two months, she was administered empiric azithromycin, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, and ciprofloxacin due to persistent symptoms. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed the presence of a complex fistulous tract suggesting bilateral ischiorectal space abscesses and a horseshoe fistula (Figures 1, 2). She was then referred to the colorectal surgery department at our institution due to persistence of the abscess.

panels.figure_caption: Preoperative transanal ultrasound showing the fistula (red arrow)
in_text_mentions: ent had undergone abscess draining and fistulotomy. Transanal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a transsphinteric fistula in the high-mid anal canal without any internal opening, and another fistula extending as far as the left internal obturator muscle (Figs. 1, 2). The patient was selected for ADSCs treatment and preoperatively prepared with daily lavage using hydrogen peroxide and sodium chloride solution. The surgical procedure was performed when the fistula had stopped discharging pus. MYSTEM® EVO Technology (MySTEM LLC, Wilmington, DE,USA) was used to obtain stem cells.
